angle: Grouped by C# 15 feature and by platform axis, so that each story delivers one user-visible capability end to end. A feature axis is one language feature seen from the user side, for example "an aspect can be applied to a union type" or "a template may contain a labeled break", and it carries the code model, the templates, the linker, the design-time pipeline, the pattern libraries and the tests for that one feature in a single pull request. A platform axis is one host or target that the platform baseline names, for example the .NET 11 SDK, the net11.0 target framework, the Visual Studio 2027 build host, or the stable Roslyn 5.12. Findings that several themes reported against the same file and the same switch statement are merged into one cluster and appear in exactly one story. Three consequences of the angle are visible in the result. First, the enabling work is separated from the features: the renumbering to Roslyn 5.12 (ST-1), the regeneration of the generated syntax model (ST-2), the language version tables (ST-3) and the variant gating decision (ST-6) are stories of their own, because every feature story is blocked on them and none of them delivers a user-visible capability by itself. Second, the union work is split by capability rather than by layer, because one pull request cannot carry the whole feature: seeing a union (ST-11), compiling a file that contains one (ST-12), advising it (ST-13 and ST-14), editing it (ST-16), overriding its synthesized members (ST-15) and the behaviour of the pattern libraries on it (ST-17). Third, defects that are not caused by C# 15 but were found while reading the same code, such as the extension block gaps of TP-7 and PR-11 or the declaration kind switches of DT-5 and PR-10, are kept in stories of their own so that they can ship independently of the Roslyn 5.12 date. Verified against the working tree: /home/user/Metalama/Metalama.Framework/src contains no reference to IsUnion or UnionDeclaration and no production `#if ROSLYN_` block, so every union story starts from zero and every one of them is gated by the decision of ST-6.

clusters.title: Hand-written syntax-kind lists that omit the union declaration
clusters.rationale: Four themes reported the same defect against the same small set of predicates. SyntaxKindExtensions.IsTypeDeclaration enumerates exactly class, struct, interface, record and record struct (Metalama.Framework/src/Metalama.Framework.Engine/Utilities/Roslyn/SyntaxKindExtensions.cs:33-35, verified), and IsBaseTypeDeclaration derives from it at :41. The same enumeration is repeated by hand in SyntaxExtensions.FindMemberDeclarationOrNull (:29-36), FindSymbolDeclaringNode (:59-66) and GetDeclaringType (:113-119). Every consequence the four themes describe follows from those five places: the wrong LAMA0048 on a partial union (SourceNamedTypeImpl.cs:329-352), the missing design-time generation (DesignTimeSyntaxTreeGenerator.cs:158-171), the suppressions that do not reach a union header, and the linker sites of LK-3. It is one edit with one shared decision about whether the predicate becomes a type test on TypeDeclarationSyntax or gains a union kind, so it must be one work item and not four.

clusters.title: The compile-time code rewriter and the templating validators have no union dispatch
clusters.rationale: Both findings name the same member switches: CompileTimeCompilationBuilder.FindCompileTimeCodeVisitor.cs:58-99 and CompileTimeCompilationBuilder.ProduceCompileTimeCodeRewriter.cs:204-210 with the private VisitTypeDeclaration at :417-435, plus the parallel switches of TemplateAnnotator and TemplatingCodeValidator.Visitor. CM-9 describes the run-time union in a file that also contains compile-time code, and TP-6 describes the union nested in a compile-time class. Both are fixed by the same dispatch, so they are one work item.

clusters.title: Syntax visitors without a union override
clusters.rationale: CM-7 is the inventory of visitors that inherit the Roslyn dispatch and therefore never see a union declaration, and LK-10 is one member of that inventory, the TextSpanClassifier, whose fix additionally requires the TemplateAnnotator to annotate the declaration so that a run-time union is not classified as compile-time. They share the mechanism and the variant gating, so they are treated as one work item and split across two stories only because the classifier belongs to the design-time capability.

clusters.title: The generated design-time partial part carries the wrong declaration keyword
clusters.rationale: Three themes reported the same arm of the same factory. DesignTimeSyntaxTreeGenerator.CreatePartialType selects a struct declaration for any TypeKind.Struct that is not a record, verified at Metalama.Framework/src/Metalama.Framework.Engine/Pipeline/DesignTime/DesignTimeSyntaxTreeGenerator.cs:749, and a union is reported by Roslyn as TypeKind.Struct, so the generated part is a partial struct and the compiler reports CS0261 in the generated document. The three findings agree on the remedy and disagree only on the discriminator and on whether the case list is repeated, which is a single decision.

clusters.title: The C# 15 language version tables of the engine
clusters.rationale: Four themes reported edits to the same two files. SupportedCSharpVersions.Latest is CSharp14 (SupportedCSharpVersions.cs:31-32, verified), All lists C# 10 to C# 14 (:38-43), ToLanguageVersion maps both V5_0_0 and V5_10_0 to CSharp14 (:57-60) and GetMaxLanguageVersion returns CSharp14 for every Roslyn 5 (:149-152). LanguageVersionExtensions.ToDisplayStringSafe has no arm for 1500 and throws. LV-2 is the throwing display mapping, LV-3 the tables, TP-2 the same tables seen from the template verifier, TP-8 the constants seen from the template language, DT-4 the design-time consequence of not touching them, and LV-6 the verification that the operator table needs nothing. One pull request edits all of it.

clusters.title: The language version of the compile-time project manifest
clusters.rationale: Both findings concern the same two fallbacks and the same dead property. CompileTimeProjectManifest.ResolvedLanguageVersion at :99-101 documents CSharp13 and is not read, while CompileTimeCompilationBuilder.cs:1355 and CompileTimeProjectRepository.Builder.cs:596 apply their own fallback. LV-5 adds the clamp that a lower Roslyn variant needs when it reads a manifest written at C# 15. The property and the clamp cannot be decided separately.

clusters.title: Regeneration of the generated syntax model from the stable grammar
clusters.rationale: TreeReader.RemoveExperimentalDeclarations strips every node carrying ExperimentalUrl before generation, so the meta syntax rewriter, the version verifier and the design-time hashers know nothing of the union declaration, the with element and the labeled break. TP-1 reports the grammar refresh, TP-9 the hashers that follow from it and DT-3 the same hashers seen from the design-time diff. One regeneration produces all three results, so they are one work item.

clusters.title: Renumbering the latest Roslyn variant to the stable 5.12
clusters.rationale: The consumed 5.10.0-1.26365.3 has no stable counterpart, so leaving the prerelease is a renumbering rather than a label edit. LV-12 decides the target version and the version strings, LV-13 enumerates the eight edit sites and the two silent failure modes, LV-14 corrects the procedure document that the renumbering follows, DT-8 is the same edit seen as a release gate for the packages published on nuget.org, and PR-1 is the mirror edit in Metalama.Premium. Performing any one of them without the others leaves the two repositories inconsistent, so they are one work item across two repositories.

clusters.title: Variant gating of the C# 15 Roslyn API members
clusters.rationale: This is a single cross-cutting decision rather than a duplicated finding, but it is listed as a cluster because at least fourteen other findings state that their implementation depends on its outcome. Verified in the working tree: /home/user/Metalama/Metalama.Framework/src contains no production `#if ROSLYN_` block, and eng/RoslynVersions/Roslyn.5.10.0.props:8-10 states that the only variant constant exists for two aspect tests. Every union or closed reference reopens that policy.

clusters.title: The .NET 11 SDK is absent from the build containers
clusters.owner_theme: UT (user target framework, patterns, tests and docs)
clusters.rationale: Three themes reported the same container gap in two repositories. eng/src/Program.cs pins one .NET SDK, verified at line 26 as the constant dotNetSdkVersion = "10.0.400" with the comment that it is the only .NET SDK required by the product. Without a second SDK component no project may target net11.0, because the .NET 10 SDK rejects the target framework outright. PR-3 and PR-8 are the same gap in Metalama.Premium, whose container was moved to Visual Studio 2026 by the merged Metalama.Premium#86 but still carries the obsolete .NET 8 SDK and .NET 6 runtime.

clusters.title: net11.0 legs across the test matrix
clusters.owner_theme: UT (user target framework, patterns, tests and docs)
clusters.rationale: Seven findings describe one coverage gap from seven angles: the test projects, the tested target framework scenario, the standalone scenarios, the design-time host simulator, the test infrastructure package pins, the MSBuild pin, and the fixed net8.0 value that the tests observe. They share one prerequisite, the container of CL-10, and one decision, whether both Core legs run or only the new one, so they are planned as one work item even though the edit touches many project files.

clusters.title: Per-declaration-kind switches in the code actions
clusters.rationale: The same shape of defect in two repositories. CSharpAttributeHelper enumerates declaration kinds and returns null for the rest, so the add-attribute code action already does nothing for records, record structs and extension blocks, and ChangeVisibilityCodeAction in Metalama.Premium enumerates type kinds and already skips interfaces and indexers. Both are repaired by testing the abstract base type instead of the kind, which also admits unions without naming an experimental member, so one decision covers both.

clusters.title: Introducing a closed class
clusters.rationale: Both findings propose the same member, INamedTypeBuilder.IsClosed, and the same emission point, the type modifier list of ModifierHelper, and both state the same three constraints: the implicit abstractness that must not be emitted, the ordering against the partial modifier, and the gating to the latest Roslyn variant. They are one work item reported by the code model theme and by the linker and advice theme.

clusters.title: Extension indexers in advice, in the linker and in the contracts
clusters.rationale: LK-6 lifts the introduction restriction that AdviceFactory enforces, LK-7 is the overriding half of the same feature, and UT-16 is the contract and test coverage that the same code model shape decides. The three cannot be validated separately, because every one of them needs the same prerequisite, namely a compilation that accepts an extension indexer.

clusters.title: Labeled break and continue in the template compiler and the linker
clusters.rationale: One feature, two failure modes and one test set. TP-3 is the annotator that drops the label and mistakes the scope, LK-9 is the inlining rewrite that copies user labels verbatim and therefore collides once labeled loops make collisions realistic, and UT-17 is the metric and observability coverage for the same syntax. The label renaming of LK-9 and the label scope of TP-3 read the same members of the break and continue statements, so they share the variant gating.

clusters.title: C# 15 in the test framework and the aspect test conventions
clusters.rationale: Three themes reported the same behaviour of TestOptions: a language version that the current Roslyn does not recognise causes the test to be skipped with a reason and no failure, so a C# 15 test suite added too early passes vacuously. LV-8 records the tolerance, DT-7 records that it hides the whole suite, and UT-19 is the convention set that follows. They are one work item in one test project.

clusters.title: Union behaviour of the pattern and extension libraries
clusters.owner_theme: UT (user target framework, patterns, tests and docs)
clusters.rationale: UT-14 is the shared preamble stating that a union is an ordinary struct for every pattern, and the four sub-findings are its consequences in Observability, Immutability, Caching and Multicast. PR-12 is the same question in the Premium architecture rules, and its only product change is in the core reference index walker. They share one prerequisite, the code model surface of ST-11, and one test matrix.

clusters.title: Documentation that states the previous baseline
clusters.owner_theme: UT (user target framework, patterns, tests and docs)
clusters.rationale: Five findings propose only prose. UT-18 is the sweep of thirteen locations that still name net8.0 or C# 14 as the latest, LV-10 is the background statement that the net10.0 literals name our own outputs and move with the Core flavour, DT-9 is the host runtime statement for the Workspaces and LinqPad packages, and PR-9 and PR-14 extend the drift point list of the platform support document to Metalama.Premium. One pull request should carry them, after the code stories have settled what the text must say.

clusters.title: Already delivered by merged pull requests
clusters.rationale: PR-15 is fully implemented by metalama/Metalama.Premium#85, merged on 2026-09-03, which dropped the Roslyn 4.12 variant, added the 5.0.0 lower variant and the 5.10.0 latest variant and added the prerelease package source. PR-4 is fully implemented by metalama/Metalama.Premium#86, merged on 2026-09-03, which retargeted the engineering project to net10.0 and removed the .NET 9 runtime from the image. Neither is new work; they are recorded so that the plan states the baseline it starts from.

stories.title: Move the latest Roslyn variant to the stable 5.12 and leave the prerelease feed
stories.rationale: This is the platform axis on which every C# 15 capability depends, and it is the only story that can start today. The consumed Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp is the prerelease 5.10.0-1.26365.3 and no stable 5.10 or 5.11 package exists, so leaving the prerelease is a renumbering of the latest variant to 5.12 rather than an edit of a version label. The user-visible capability is that the published Metalama.Framework.Workspaces, Metalama.Testing.AspectTesting and Metalama.LinqPad packages restore from nuget.org again, which is the regression that issue #1106 already produced once. The work is the eight edit sites of LV-13, in two steps as LV-12 describes: a prerelease step as soon as Metalama.Compiler builds on 5.12, then the stable step that removes the roslyn-consolidated source by removing the hyphen from SupportedCSharpVersions.ToNuGetVersionString. Two ordering constraints must be respected inside the pull request. The generator version list is ordered and the enum value of each variant is its index, so the retired 5.10.0 name has to be inserted in version order in the legacy list rather than appended. The variant constant is hardcoded as ROSLYN_5_10_0_OR_GREATER in eng/RoslynVersions/Roslyn.5.10.0.props:10 (verified) and has to be renamed with the variant. LV-14 corrects the procedure document in the same pull request, because updating-roslyn.md step 10 names members that no longer exist. PR-1 performs the mirror renumbering in Metalama.Premium, which must ship in the same release or the two repositories disagree about the variant name and the package source. The external prerequisite, Metalama.Compiler moving to Roslyn 5.12, is not verifiable from this session and is the reason the story is listed as touching that repository.

stories.title: Regenerate the syntax model from the C# 15 grammar and guard the experimental nodes
stories.rationale: One platform axis: the generated half of the engine must know the C# 15 syntax before any feature story can use it. TreeReader.RemoveExperimentalDeclarations strips every node marked ExperimentalUrl, so the meta syntax rewriter, the version verifier and the design-time hashers currently know nothing of the union declaration, the with element or the labeled break, and the hashers therefore miss a design-time edit, which is a silent staleness rather than an error. Adding Syntax-5.12.0.xml as a new file, as updating-roslyn.md requires, and regenerating produces all of it at once: the rewriter members, the verifier overrides that report the version specific node diagnostic, and the hasher cases. Three items ride with the regeneration because they exist only as a consequence of it. TP-4 is the with element, whose only remaining work after regeneration is a test, and the finding corrects the test path: the file belongs beside Tests/Aspects/CSharp12/CollectionExpressions.cs, not in a Syntax/CollectionExpressions directory that does not exist. TP-9 and DT-3 add the two hasher test cases. TP-5 is the guard that survives the regeneration, because the unsafe expression keeps its experimental marker on Roslyn main and stays stripped, so the template compiler needs a name free rejection driven by the generator rather than a per-node override. The proposed grammar drift check of TP-1 has to be reformulated as a comparison against the grammar of the exact consumed package, because a check keyed on the prerelease label would never pass while the unsafe expression stays experimental.

stories.title: Accept C# 15 as a supported language version of the engine
stories.rationale: The user-visible capability is that a project with LangVersion 15.0 builds with Metalama instead of being reported as unsupported. Verified today: SupportedCSharpVersions.Latest is CSharp14 (SupportedCSharpVersions.cs:31-32), All lists C# 10 to C# 14 (:38-43), ToLanguageVersion maps both V5_0_0 and V5_10_0 to CSharp14 (:57-60), and GetMaxLanguageVersion returns CSharp14 for every Roslyn 5 (:149-152). The pull request adds AllLanguageVersions.CSharp15 as the numeric cast 1500, adds the 1500 arm to ToDisplayStringSafe so that LAMA0051 and LAMA0052 are formatted instead of throwing (LV-2), makes Latest variant aware rather than a shared constant, and maps only the renumbered latest variant to CSharp15, because the Roslyn 5.0 variant that serves Rider rejects 1500. The version boundary in GetMaxLanguageVersion is 5.12 and not 5.10: a Roslyn 5.10 compiler has no such language version, so the more permissive arm would over-state the capability of a desktop MSBuild. LV-4 and LV-5 travel with it, because the manifest fallback and the reading clamp decide what a lower variant does with a library whose templates were compiled at C# 15, and the clamp cannot be written before Latest is variant aware. TP-2 and TP-8 are the same tables seen from the template verifier and from the template language pin, and DT-4 records the deliberate non-change at design time, namely that the design-time pipeline verifies no language version and does not need to. LV-6 closes with no code change: the operator table needs nothing, because C# 15 adds no user definable operator.

stories.title: Let a test request C# 15, and make a lost language version fail instead of skipping
stories.rationale: The capability is for the team rather than for the user, and it must land before any feature story writes a test, otherwise the whole C# 15 suite passes vacuously. TestOptions parses the language version directive and, when the running Roslyn does not recognise the value, marks the test skipped with a reason and reports no failure. That tolerance is correct while C# 15 does not exist, which is what LV-8 records, and dangerous afterwards, which is what DT-7 records. The pull request adds the CSharp15 directive support, gives the aspect test project and the unit test context a way to request the version, and introduces the convention set of UT-19: a Tests/Aspects/CSharp15 directory whose metalamaTests.json carries the required constant of the renumbered latest variant, and a per file language version directive. The constant name follows the renumbering of ST-1, so the gate is the 5.12 constant and not the 5.10 one. The Patterns aspect tests need no gate, because they run only against the latest engine.

stories.title: A net11.0 project keeps the C# 15 that its SDK implies
stories.rationale: This is the last step of the user-visible language version capability, and it lives in MSBuild rather than in the engine. Verified in the working tree: Metalama.Framework.targets rewrites LangVersion to 12.0 whenever Metalama.Compiler reports that the value was implicitly set and the value is not one of 12.0, 13.0, 14.0, default, latest, latestMajor or preview (lines 117-120), and the warning that explains it is emitted by the MetalamaCheckLangVersion target at line 243 with no diagnostic code. When the implied value becomes 15.0, a net11.0 project therefore drops three language versions at once, to C# 12, and the warning text states the reason falsely. The pull request extends the accepted value list with 15.0, gives the Warning task the Code attribute that it supports so that the warning can be suppressed through MSBuildWarningsAsMessages, corrects the message, and adds the standalone scenario Standalone/DefaultLanguageVersion/DotNet11. The scenario needs the .NET 11 SDK in the container, which is why the story is blocked on ST-7, and its existing sibling still carries a comment that speaks of .NET 8 and C# 12 (DotNet.csproj:3, verified) although the project targets net10.0 at line 6, so that comment is corrected in the same change. LV-7 rides along as the comment that records why the repository keeps its own LangMaxVersion at 14.0 while raising what it supports, and states the two separate bounds that are otherwise confused. One open question remains for the product owner and is listed as a decision: whether Metalama.Compiler computes the implied version from its own table, in which case the clamp may never fire for net11.0.

stories.title: Decide and implement how engine source names the C# 15 Roslyn API members
stories.rationale: This is a decision with a small proof of concept, and it is the gate of every union and closed story. The constraint is verified: the Metalama.Framework.Engine.5.0.0 project compiles the same source files against Roslyn 5.0, which has neither the union syntax node nor ITypeSymbol.IsUnion, and /home/user/Metalama/Metalama.Framework/src contains no production `#if ROSLYN_` block today, while eng/RoslynVersions/Roslyn.5.10.0.props:8-10 states that the single variant constant exists only for two aspect tests. Three mechanisms are available and they are not interchangeable: conditional compilation, which is the only one that can override a virtual method or call a syntax factory; numeric syntax kind values with a runtime guard, which name no experimental member and compile in both variants; and a per variant service that answers the three symbol questions. The decision has to be taken once, because at least fourteen findings state that their implementation depends on it, and a mixed answer would leave the same feature gated three different ways. The pull request records the choice in Directory.Packages.md beside the existing variant doctrine and implements one representative site so that the pattern is copyable. It also settles the second half of the question, namely what the Roslyn 5.0 variant does when it meets a union or a closed type that comes from a referenced assembly.

stories.title: Install the .NET 11 SDK in the build containers and repair the SDK ceiling check
stories.rationale: One platform axis, and the prerequisite of every net11.0 test. The container pins a single .NET SDK: eng/src/Program.cs:26 declares the constant dotNetSdkVersion = "10.0.400" and the comment at lines 19-25 explains that two feature bands make MSBuildExtensionsPath resolve to a different SDK directory and produce MSB4062, so a second component must be added together with the mitigation described in CLAUDE.md. The story also carries the one-line defect that the missing coverage hides, and that defect is user-visible today. Metalama.Framework.props:33 sets MaximumSdkVersion to 11.0, and Metalama.Framework.targets:410-413 compares the full SDK version with VersionGreaterThan, so every .NET 11 SDK, including 11.0.100, reports LAMA0601 saying that the SDK is newer than 11.0, which contradicts the very matrix that issue #1884 declared. The repair is a second property that truncates the SDK version to major and minor for the maximum rule only, because the minimum rule legitimately keeps feature band precision. On the Premium side, the container was already moved to Visual Studio 2026 by the merged Metalama.Premium#86, so PR-3 is reduced to removing the obsolete .NET 8 SDK and .NET 6 runtime components and the stale Visual Studio 2022 channel manifest, and deciding whether the prerelease flag follows the core repository. PR-8 is the Premium half of the same SDK leg.

stories.title: Run the test matrix on net11.0
stories.rationale: One platform axis, delivered as evidence rather than as a feature: net11.0 is a declared supported target framework and nothing in the repository builds or runs against it. The work is a second Core leg on the test projects, the two missing rows of the tested target framework scenario, a net11.0 variant of the standalone scenarios whose behaviour depends on the runtime, a net11.0 target for the design-time host simulator with the simulator target framework following the build SDK rather than a constant, and the verification that Microsoft.Build.Locator still resolves the MSBuild of the .NET 11 SDK into a process compiled against the 18.0.2 reference assemblies. Two corrections from the findings shape the scope. The MSBuild pin stays at 18.0.2, because the doctrine is to pin to the lowest supported host and the verification is what the leg provides. UT-4 must land first inside the story, because DefaultProjectOptions reports a fixed net8.0 to every test, so the tests cannot observe their own leg until that value follows the real target framework; the aspect test harness composes one expected file per test with no target framework in its name, so a leg dependent value has to be pinned rather than made variable. The size is L because the number of expected output files that may diverge between the two legs is not known in advance.

stories.title: Move the build host baseline to the November 2026 Visual Studio
stories.rationale: One platform axis, small and externally gated. eng/src/Program.cs pins VisualStudioBuildToolsComponentVersion.v18_9_2 at line 40 (verified) and MSBuildVersion accordingly, which is the current Visual Studio 2026 quarterly release and not the November 2026 baseline that PB-2027.0 names. The change is three constants, and it cannot be made until PostSharp.Engineering exposes the newer Build Tools component version, which is the reason issue #1902 declined the previous move. The story also carries the November 2026 measurement that Metalama.Framework.props:34-37 already schedules, namely reading the feature band and the Visual Studio floor once the long-term servicing baseline ships, and it should be scheduled together with the ceiling re-reading that Directory.Packages.md already dates after 2026-11-10, so that one measurement session serves both.

stories.title: Remove the residue of the previous platform baseline from the engine and the test suites
stories.rationale: One platform axis, hygiene, and independent of every C# 15 date. Four unrelated leftovers of the move that dropped .NET 8 and .NET 9 share one property: each is invisible in a normal build and none produces a failure. The default target frameworks of the nested compile-time reference project still name net8.0, so an additional compile-time package resolves its netstandard2.0 asset instead of its net10.0 asset and an out-of-support target framework is restored on every build. Two facts in the Contracts unit tests are excluded on every leg because their guard names NET6_0 rather than NET6_0_OR_GREATER, and two aspect tests never run because their guard names a Roslyn constant that no variant defines and that is misspelled without underscores. The dependency pins need no version change for .NET 11, but three audit suppressions are probably dead and several comments state rules that no longer hold. Each item is minutes of work; grouping them keeps them from being forgotten and gives one place to re-run the vulnerability audit under the new SDK.

stories.title: An aspect can see a union type in the code model
stories.rationale: The first union capability and the foundation of all the others: the code model must be able to say that a type is a union, to name its case types, and to answer that a partial union is partial. Today it cannot. A union is reported by Roslyn as an ordinary struct, so INamedType exposes no way to tell it apart, and every hand-written syntax-kind list treats the declaration as unknown. Verified: SyntaxKindExtensions.IsTypeDeclaration enumerates exactly class, struct, interface, record and record struct (SyntaxKindExtensions.cs:33-35), which is why IsPartial returns false for a partial union and LAMA0048 is reported wrongly, why the design-time partial file is never generated, and why a suppression placed on a union header does not apply. The pull request adds IsUnion and the case types to INamedType next to IsRecord, without a new TypeKind value because the two record TypeKind members are already obsolete for exactly that reason, widens the five shared predicates, and adds the visitor overrides of the inventory. Every one of these edits names a Roslyn member that the 5.0 variant does not have, so the story is blocked on ST-6 and on the renumbering. The size is L because the predicate change has many consumers that must each be reviewed, in particular the two sites where a union case list would be mistaken for a parameter list. The design-time generator half of DT-1 is deliberately not here; it is the subject of ST-16.

stories.title: A file that declares a union and an aspect compiles
stories.rationale: The second union capability, and the one that produces the most confusing failure if it is left out. The compile-time code rewriter classifies members by declaration kind and copies the rest verbatim, so a run-time union that happens to sit in a file that also contains compile-time code is copied into the compile-time compilation, where it fails with a message about a language version or a missing framework type rather than about the real cause, and a union nested in a compile-time class is copied verbatim while a union nested in a run-time class is dropped silently. The remedy is one dispatch in ProduceCompileTimeCodeRewriter routed to the existing private VisitTypeDeclaration, which already classifies by templating scope, plus the same recognition in the compile-time code finder, the template annotator and the templating code validator. A type test that excludes extension blocks avoids naming the union node at all, which is the cheapest answer to the gating question, and the story should follow whichever mechanism ST-6 chose. The acceptance test is one aspect test that puts a run-time union and an aspect in the same file.

stories.title: Advice applied to a union is injected and linked
stories.rationale: The third union capability: an aspect that adds a method to a union must produce that method. The injection rewriter and the linking rewriter both dispatch on the concrete type declaration kinds, so an injected member targeting a union is never inserted, and once the injection is repaired the linking step must also visit the declaration or the injected members reference helpers that were never emitted, which is a build error in generated code. The two rewriters are one pull request because repairing only the first produces a worse state than repairing neither. Two details decide correctness. The fallback for an unknown type declaration must preserve the parameter list, because for a union that list holds the case types, and it must not be routed through the record or struct rewrite paths, which pass a default parameter list when a primary constructor was removed and would therefore delete the cases. The dispatch should be written against the abstract type declaration so that the shared source still compiles for the Roslyn 5.0 variant.

stories.title: Advice that a union cannot carry is refused with a clear diagnostic
stories.rationale: This is the defensive slice of the union feature and the one item that should ship even if the rest of the union work slips, which is why it is a story of its own. The language forbids instance fields, auto-properties and field-like events in a union, forbids a public single-parameter constructor, and requires every explicit constructor to chain to a compiler-generated one. An aspect that introduces a backing field or a constructor therefore produces code that the compiler rejects with an error reported on generated code, which is the worst diagnostic experience Metalama can offer. One blanket eligibility rule that declares a union ineligible as an advice target costs a single diagnostic and covers all three compiler errors as well as the silent case where an initializer is injected into a constructor that has no syntax. The rule reads the code model member added by ST-11 rather than the Roslyn symbol, because the eligibility rules live in the public assembly, which does not reference Roslyn. Per-advice rules are the better long-term answer and are the alternative option recorded in the decisions.

stories.title: The compiler-synthesized union members are visible and overridable
stories.rationale: The fourth union capability, and the one with an external dependency. A union carries a synthesized Value property and one constructor per case, and the code model reaches them through paths that assume a known declaration syntax: the declaration flag reader has a throwing default arm for an unexpected declaration kind, and the record helpers are keyed on the record declaration kinds. An aspect that touches Value therefore fails with an assertion rather than with a diagnostic. The mechanism that materializes compiler-synthesized members already exists in the open pull request metalama/Metalama#1879 for records, and every gate of it is keyed on IsRecord, so this story is an extension of that mechanism and must be based on it rather than reimplement it. It is separated from ST-11 because it can be deferred without making the rest of the union support incorrect: until it lands, ST-14 refuses the advice that would reach these members.

stories.title: A union with introduced members is correct in the editor
stories.rationale: The fifth union capability, and the one the user sees first, because it is the design-time experience. The generated partial part is produced by a factory that selects a struct declaration for any struct that is not a record, verified at DesignTimeSyntaxTreeGenerator.cs:749, and a union is reported as a struct, so the generated document declares a partial struct against a partial union and the editor shows CS0261 on the type. The pull request adds a union arm that emits a union declaration with a null parameter list, because at most one partial part may carry the case list, and the same change routes the text span classifier so that a compile-time union is classified. The classifier fix has to be made in two places, because routing every unhandled type declaration to the compile-time helper would classify a run-time union, a run-time interface and an extension block as compile-time; the template annotator must annotate the declaration first. One open question decides the shape of the arm and is listed in the decisions, namely whether a partial part may omit the case list.

stories.title: The pattern and extension libraries behave correctly on a union
stories.rationale: The last union capability, seen from the aspect libraries that a user actually applies. Because a union is an ordinary struct for every pattern, most of the behaviour is already correct and needs only to be pinned by tests: the observability aspect rejects it with its existing message, and the multicast selector treats it as a struct target. Three items are real work. The immutability classification calls a union mutable, which produces spurious observability warnings, and the rule must key on the union declaration rather than on the Roslyn union flag, because that flag is also true for a hand-written type carrying the union attribute whose state is unconstrained. The caching layer keys and serializes a union as an opaque struct, which is a silent wrong result, and the discriminator is the implicitly implemented union interface rather than an attribute lookup; the formatter projects target frameworks that do not have that interface, so the check has to be made by name at run time or the projects need a new leg. The multicast constructor target produces an invalid constructor. PR-12 needs no Premium product change, only a reference index walker override in the core so that a case type reference is attributed rather than dropped, plus two architecture tests. The size is L because five libraries and two repositories are touched.

stories.title: Closed hierarchies end to end
stories.rationale: One C# 15 feature, and the smallest of them, because the derived closedness is already modelled correctly everywhere. The capability has two halves that belong in one pull request. Reading: INamedType gains IsClosed, and the documentation of the derived types options records that for a closed type declared in the current compilation the direct enumeration is exhaustive. Writing: INamedTypeBuilder gains IsClosed with the validation that mirrors the compiler rules, and the type modifier list emits the closed token instead of the abstract token, because an explicit abstract on a closed class is itself an error and the compiler applies the abstractness implicitly. Two constraints are external and decide the schedule. The type symbol member that carries the value does not exist in the Roslyn 5.0 variant and is marked experimental in the consumed build, so the read is gated by ST-6. The emission requires a compilation at C# 15, so it is gated by ST-3. TP-10 closes with no work for the template compiler and the syntax generator, with one caveat worth recording: after the compile-time language version rises, a closed class in compile-time code needs two attributes that the compiler does not synthesize and that the netstandard reference set does not provide. UT-15 adds the pattern library tests that keep the generated output under observation.

stories.title: Extension indexers end to end
stories.rationale: One C# 15 feature, complete in one pull request because its three halves share a single prerequisite. Introducing an indexer into an extension block is refused today by an explicit validation, and that refusal was documented rather than lifted when issue #1587 corrected the XML summary, so the user-visible change is that the refusal is replaced by an eligibility rule that enforces the rules the language actually imposes: a named receiver parameter, no init accessor, and none of the modifiers the proposal forbids. Overriding an indexer that already exists in source follows the extension property path and is expected to be correct when the override is inlineable; the non-inlined case is refused by the existing linker diagnostic, which is the subject of the separate open issue #937 and bounds what the tests can assert. The contract advice and the not-null fabric need no product change but need tests, and before writing them the story must determine whether the fabric enumeration reaches an extension block at all, because the indexer is a member of the block rather than of the enclosing static class. The whole story is unwritable before C# 15 is a requestable language version, which is why it is blocked on ST-3 and not on the union work.

stories.title: Labeled break and continue end to end
stories.rationale: One C# 15 feature with two independent failure modes, which is why it is one story rather than two. In the template compiler the label is not modelled: the annotator has no visit for a labeled statement, so the scope of the labeled loop is not propagated and the generated rewriter drops the label, which silently retargets the break to the innermost loop. After regeneration the same case produces a compiler error in transformed user code instead, which is an improvement but still wrong. The fix records label to scope in the annotator context, annotates the break and continue statements from the label, and reports a new template diagnostic when a run-time break targets a compile-time loop; only the immediately nested statement is labeled, and a labeled continue may target only an iteration statement, so the mapping must be restricted accordingly. In the linker the second failure mode is that inlining copies user labels verbatim, so a template label and a target label can collide and produce a compiler error in the transformed compilation; labeled loops make that collision realistic for the first time. The fix is a label renaming substitution that allocates unique names through the existing lexical scope factory. UT-17 adds the metric and observability tests, which can be written before C# 15 is enabled if the compilation ignores the feature diagnostic.

stories.title: Every declaration kind is reachable by the code actions
stories.rationale: A user-visible defect that exists today, independently of C# 15, and that a union would silently join. Both code actions enumerate declaration kinds and do nothing for the kinds they do not name, so the add-attribute refactoring already fails on records, record structs and extension blocks, and the change-visibility fix already fails on interfaces and indexers. In both cases the remedy is to test the abstract base type instead of the kind, which fixes the present defects, admits unions later without naming an experimental member, and removes the per-kind maintenance obligation that has already been paid once per kind. Two cautions belong in the pull request: the fallback must be narrowed so that it does not admit namespaces, enum members or incomplete members, for which an added attribute list would be invalid, and the trivia-preserving behaviour that issue #779 established must not regress. Shipping this before the union stories means that the union case costs nothing later.

stories.title: Close the two extension block gaps that predate C# 15
stories.rationale: Two defects found while reading the C# 15 code paths that have nothing to do with C# 15 and can ship at any time, which is exactly why they are kept out of the feature stories. A template declared inside an extension block in a compile-time class is copied verbatim by the compile-time rewriter, because the member switch has no case for the extension block declaration; either the member loop is extracted and reused, which is the support option, or a diagnostic is reported, which is the cheap option. Reusing the type declaration path unchanged is not sufficient, because Roslyn makes an extension block declaration behave unlike other type declarations: its identifier is default, its base list is null, and the corresponding with-methods throw. In Metalama.Premium, the reference validation context throws for a validated extension block because the declaration kind has no granularity mapping, and the exception surfaces as an error diagnostic inside the user validator. That is reachable by a customer of the current release, since extension blocks are a C# 14 feature that already ships, and the core repository already repaired the same class of defect once in issue #1339.

stories.title: Execute the Roslyn 5.0 variant of the Premium engines
stories.rationale: One platform axis in the Premium repository. The Roslyn 5.0 variant of the validation and code fix engines is compiled by the solution but no test ever loads it, so a defect that appears only when those engines bind against the older Roslyn reaches a Rider user before it reaches the team. The previous lower variant served a host that was also covered by manual Visual Studio 2022 testing; the 5.0 variant serves no host that anyone tests by hand, so the gap is materially worse than it was. Adding variant test projects is necessary but not sufficient, because the sibling test projects reference the unsuffixed engine by a hardcoded path and would load the latest engine while compiling under the older property set; they must first be made variant aware in the way the core aspect test project already is. The unit test shims additionally need a lower-variant build of the core unit test helper package, which is a core change and the reason the unit test half is larger. PR-13 corrects the comment in those same project files, which now describes a variant constant that no longer exists.

stories.title: Premium build-file hygiene
stories.rationale: Residue that the Premium alignment deliberately left out of scope, grouped so that it is not lost. The template language version is pinned at C# 13 with a rationale that names a Visual Studio version rather than the Roslyn floor, and the blocker for raising it, the older Roslyn variant, was removed by the merged alignment pull request; the rewritten comment must name the lowest declared variant rather than copy the core comment verbatim, because the property the core comment cites does not exist in this repository. Two MSBuild package pins lag the core doctrine and one references a package that does not exist and that nothing consumes. The Redis client is pinned twice, so the version update is inert and the backend ships against the older client, which is a silent behaviour difference rather than a build failure. None of these blocks anything; together they are half a day.

stories.title: Document PB-2027.0 and the C# 15 scope
stories.rationale: One documentation pull request, scheduled last because it can only state what the code stories decided. It corrects the locations that still name net8.0 or C# 14 as the latest, the standalone project comments that describe a check which was since disabled, and the release notes; it records that the net10.0 literals in the engine name our own outputs rather than the SDK and move only with the embedded Core flavour; it states in the Workspaces and LinqPad package documentation that the host runtime major decides which SDK the in-process MSBuild registration may use, so that a user on a machine carrying only the newer SDK understands the failure; and it extends the drift point list of the platform support document from Metalama.Compiler to Metalama.Premium, which repeats the compared target framework literal in eight build files with no test to catch a value left behind. One item of the sweep must be split out and treated as behaviour rather than prose, and it is called out here so that it is not lost in a documentation review: the well-known source generator attribute list is functional and decides whether a partial member generated by a source generator is eligible for aspects, so an attribute added by a newer framework and missing from the list changes eligibility with no diagnostic. The audience paragraph of the package version document is already owned by the open issue #1903 and must be referenced rather than rewritten here.

stories.title: Premium variant set and engineering baseline, already delivered
stories.rationale: Recorded as already in progress, and in fact already merged, so that the plan states the baseline it starts from and so that no new work is proposed for it. metalama/Metalama.Premium#85 merged on 2026-09-03 and closed issue #1913: it removed the Roslyn 4.12 variant, made 5.0.0 the lower variant with a project suffix, added the 5.10.0 latest variant, added the prerelease package source with its source mapping, and moved every target framework to net10.0. metalama/Metalama.Premium#86 merged the same day: it retargeted the engineering project to net10.0 with the vulnerability suppressions that the newer build tools assets require, removed the .NET 9 runtime from the image, and moved the container to the Visual Studio 2026 Build Tools. The residual items that those two pull requests did not cover are carried by ST-1, ST-7, ST-23 and ST-24, and are not repeated here.

decisions: Does C# 15 support ship in 2027.0 at all? The whole feature axis depends on a Roslyn that Metalama does not consume today. Verified: the consumed Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp is the prerelease 5.10.0-1.26365.3, no stable 5.10 or 5.11 package exists on nuget.org, and LanguageVersion.CSharp15 was added to Roslyn main only on 2026-08-11, so the first stable Roslyn that exposes C# 15 as a non-preview language version is expected to be 5.12, shipping in November 2026 with Visual Studio 2027 and the .NET 11 SDK, against a general availability date of 2027-01-01. Option A, full C# 15 support in 2027.0: the language version stories (ST-3, ST-4, ST-5) and all five feature stories (ST-11 to ST-21) must be written, reviewed and tested in the six to eight weeks between the stable Roslyn and general availability, and they cannot start before Metalama.Compiler moves, which is a repository this analysis could not read. Option B, C# 15 language version only: ship ST-1 to ST-5 so that a project set to C# 15 builds and its templates stay at C# 14, plus the defensive slice ST-14 so that advice on a union is refused with a clear diagnostic rather than producing uncompilable code, and defer the feature work to 2027.1. Option C, no C# 15 in 2027.0: leave the language version tables at C# 14 and accept that every net11.0 project at the SDK default is clamped to C# 12 with a warning, which is the current behaviour of the MSBuild clamp and is a three-version regression, not a one-version one. Option C is only tenable if the clamp of ST-5 is fixed to clamp to C# 14 rather than to C# 12. The consequence of Option A that should decide it is that no part of the feature work can be validated before the stable Roslyn exists, because a test that requests C# 15 today is skipped and reports success.

How is the union and closed API gated between the Roslyn 5.0 variant and the latest variant? This is the single decision that at least fourteen findings depend on, and it must be taken before any union code is written. Verified constraints: the same engine sources are compiled for both variants, Roslyn 5.0 has neither the union syntax node nor the union and closed symbol members, the members that do exist in the consumed build are marked experimental and are therefore errors by default, the repository currently has zero production conditional-compilation blocks, and the single variant constant is documented as existing only for two aspect tests. Option A, conditional compilation on the variant constant: it is the only mechanism that can override a virtual visitor method or call a syntax factory, so ST-16 and parts of ST-11 need it in any case; the cost is reopening a policy that issue #1881 deliberately closed by removing 177 such blocks, and the constant has to be renamed with every variant renumbering. Option B, numeric syntax kind values behind a runtime guard: it names no experimental member and compiles unchanged in both variants, and it covers every kind test, but it cannot override a method and it hardcodes numbers whose meaning is not visible at the call site. Option C, a per-variant service that answers the three symbol questions: it is the cleanest for the symbol reads, and it is the mechanism that issue #1215 deliberately removed from the symbol extensions on the grounds that reflection costs run-time overhead and is harder to maintain. The likely answer is a documented mixture, Option B for kind tests and Option A for the factory calls and visitor overrides, but the mixture must be written down once rather than decided per site, or the same feature ends up gated three different ways.

What does the Roslyn 5.0 variant do when it meets a union or a closed type that comes from a referenced assembly? The 5.0 variant serves Rider and the C# Dev Kit and cannot parse or represent these constructs, but it can be handed a compiled library that contains them. Option A, report false from every new code model member and continue: the user sees an aspect behave differently in Rider than in the build, with no explanation. Option B, report a diagnostic that names the host as unable to serve the feature, following the precedent of issue #1898, which degrades to no implementation when the host Roslyn is below the supported floor. Option C, decline the latest payload for such projects entirely. The consequence to weigh is that Rider is a supported design-time host of PB-2027.0, so a silent difference between the editor and the build is a support burden that lasts the whole release.

Does the template language rise to C# 15, and what happens to Rider users if it does? The template language pin is bounded by the lowest Roslyn variant, because a compile-time assembly compiled at C# 15 cannot be parsed by the Roslyn 5.0 host that serves Rider 2026.2. Option A, keep the template language at C# 14 for 2027.0: aspect authors cannot use unions, closed classes or labeled breaks inside templates, but every supported host can build every aspect library. Option B, raise it to C# 15 as an opt-in property, default C# 14: authors who opt in accept that their library cannot be built inside Rider. Option C, raise the default: the compile-time compilation of such a project fails inside Rider with a compiler error about an unsupported language version, which is a hard failure and not a degradation. Option A is the conservative answer and is what the current comment in the build properties already implies; the decision should be recorded next to that comment rather than left implicit.

For a union that an aspect targets, is the 2027.0 answer a blanket refusal or per-advice rules? The language forbids instance fields, auto-properties, field-like events, a public single-parameter constructor and a constructor that does not chain, so several ordinary advices produce code that the compiler rejects, and the error is reported on generated code. Option A, one blanket eligibility rule that makes a union ineligible as an advice target: one diagnostic, covers all three compiler errors and the silent injected-initializer case, and can ship before the rest of the union work. Option B, per-advice rules that permit what a union can carry, for example an introduced method or a static member, and refuse only what it cannot: more work, and each rule is a place where the language rules can be misread. Option A is recommended for 2027.0 with Option B as the follow-up, but the choice determines whether ST-14 is a half-day story or a two-day story and whether the union support advertised in the release notes is described as read-only.

Are introduced unions and introduced closed classes in scope? These are two separate answers. Introducing a closed class is a modifier flag on the type builder and one token in the modifier list, and it follows the precedent of the merged support for introducing a partial class, so it is small. Introducing a union requires the case list, the synthesized members and the member restrictions, and no existing builder produces a type whose members the compiler generates, so it is a large piece of work of the same size as the whole reading side. Option A, closed only: a coherent half-feature, and the reading side of unions still works. Option B, both: the union half alone is more than the rest of the union work put together. Option C, neither: the code model exposes the constructs but aspects cannot create them, which is the same position the product already holds for structs, records and enums through the open issues #869, #867 and #866. Option A is recommended; the decision determines the scope of ST-18 and whether a new introduction issue is filed at all.

Is a net11.0 test leg worth its cost in this release? Adding it requires a second .NET SDK in the build container, which the project's own written experience says costs at least one continuous integration cycle per mistake, and it doubles the Core leg of every test project with an unknown number of expected output files that may diverge. Option A, full matrix on both Core legs: highest confidence, highest cost, and the only way to observe the C# 15 default of the .NET 11 SDK. Option B, net11.0 on the standalone scenarios only: the standalone scenarios are where the SDK behaviour actually differs, and the unit and aspect tests exercise the engine rather than the SDK, so this captures most of the value for a fraction of the cost. Option C, no leg, and rely on the separate SDK matrix repository. The consequence that argues against Option C is that the supported platform check already declares the .NET 11 SDK and net11.0 as supported, and that claim is currently untested; the consequence that argues against Option A is that the net11.0 leg tells nothing new about the engine.

Which .NET SDK does the generated pin name once two are installed? The container currently pins one SDK and the comment at eng/src/Program.cs:19-25 records that two feature bands in one image already produced a build failure through a stale environment variable. Option A, keep the pin on the .NET 10 SDK and use the .NET 11 SDK only for the scenarios that request it: the product build stays reproducible and the known failure mode is avoided, but a developer whose machine carries only the newer SDK cannot run the build at all. Option B, pin the .NET 11 SDK: the product build then uses a compiler whose default language version differs from the one the tests assume. The mitigation for the known failure mode lives in PostSharp.Engineering and is incomplete by one environment variable, so this decision also determines whether that shared package must be released first.

Does the platform baseline move to the November 2026 Visual Studio in 2027.0? The build container pins the Visual Studio 2026 quarterly release 18.9, while PB-2027.0 names the November 2026 long-term servicing baseline as the floor and schedules the feature band measurement after 2026-11-10. The previous proposal to move the container was closed as not planned on the grounds that regenerating the Visual Studio base images is expensive. Option A, move once the newer Build Tools component version is exposed by PostSharp.Engineering, and take the scheduled measurement in the same session. Option B, stay on 18.9 and accept that the declared floor is never exercised. The decision is external as much as internal, because the component version must exist in the shared engineering package before the change can be made, and the same measurement is already owed by the package ceiling doctrine, so doing the two together is cheaper than doing either alone.

May the public SDK surface name the new syntax kinds? The syntax kind helper is part of the public extensibility surface, so admitting the union kind to it makes a C# 15 construct visible to extension authors, and whichever gating mechanism is chosen becomes part of that public contract. Option A, admit it: extension authors can write kind tests that behave identically to ours. Option B, keep the new kinds internal and expose only the code model member: the public surface stays independent of the Roslyn variant, at the cost of extension authors writing their own tests. The consequence to weigh is that the public surface cannot easily be narrowed later, and that an extension compiled against the latest variant and loaded into the lower one is exactly the silent failure mode that the extension loader already has, since a non-matching extension assembly is dropped without a diagnostic.
